title: SSH Brute-Force & Password Guessing Incident Response Playbook
summary: Standard operating procedure for investigating and containing high-volume automated SSH authentication failure bursts.
investigation_steps: 1. Verify the originating IP address in external threat intelligence databases (AbuseIPDB, VirusTotal).
2. Calculate failure rate and total duration of the authentication burst.
3. Inspect whether any targeted accounts are valid local users versus non-existent accounts.
4. Verify whether any authentication attempt from the attacker IP resulted in a successful session (Accepted password/publickey).
5. Inspect other hosts in the enterprise network to determine if the same source IP is targeting other exposed services.
containment_actions: 1. Implement temporary or permanent drop rule for originating IP on perimeter firewall (iptables / AWS Security Group).
2. Ensure fail2ban or dynamic rate-limiting service is functioning on the targeted host.
3. If legitimate accounts were targeted, notify account owners and review recent activity.
remediation_actions: 1. Disable password-based SSH authentication in /etc/ssh/sshd_config (PasswordAuthentication no).
2. Require SSH keys with passphrase protection and hardware tokens (FIDO2).
3. Restrict SSH access to authorized VPN gateways or bastion jump hosts.
references: NIST Special Publication 800-61 Revision 2: Computer Security Incident Handling Guide, Section 3.2

title: Compromised Valid Account & Unauthorized Access Playbook
summary: Emergency playbook for situations where repeated authentication failures precede an accepted login session.
investigation_steps: 1. Immediately isolate the affected host from the internal network while preserving volatile memory (RAM).
2. Determine exact timestamp of the successful login (pam_unix session opened).
3. Audit all commands executed during the session via shell history (.bash_history), auditd logs, or process creation events.
4. Check for persistence mechanisms added during session: new cron jobs, modified ~/.ssh/authorized_keys, new sudoers entries, or newly created accounts.
5. Identify any outbound network connections initiated by the user session (potential reverse shells or data staging).
containment_actions: 1. Terminate all active SSH sessions and processes belonging to the compromised user account.
3. Revoke all active session tokens, Kerberos tickets, and SSH authorized keys for the account.
remediation_actions: 1. Force credential reset and re-enrollment of Multi-Factor Authentication (MFA).
2. Re-image or restore the compromised host from a known clean backup if root privileges were attained.
3. Audit surrounding systems accessible with the compromised credentials.
references: NIST Special Publication 800-61 Revision 2, Section 3.3 (Containment, Eradication, and Recovery)

title: User Enumeration & Account Reconnaissance Playbook
summary: Guidance for assessing and countering systematic account discovery across identity directories.
investigation_steps: 1. Collate the full list of distinct usernames tested by the remote host.
2. Cross-reference tested usernames against valid organizational employee and service account directories.
3. Determine if the adversary obtained an internal username list (e.g., from public LinkedIn scraping or prior breaches).
4. Assess whether the attacker switched to password spraying against the identified valid accounts.
containment_actions: 1. Block or rate-limit the probing IP address.
2. Alert SOC monitoring team to flag future logins for any of the discovered valid usernames.
3. Verify that public login endpoints return generic error messages (e.g. 'Invalid credentials') that do not disclose whether a username exists.
remediation_actions: 1. Remove default accounts (guest, test, demo, oracle) from systems.
2. Implement network access control lists (ACLs) to hide administrative interfaces from public internet exposure.
references: MITRE D3FEND: D3-BAA (Biometric Authentication), D3-UD (User Account Disabling)
